name: Aaron Novak

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential, so tell me what you would say publicly and what you actually think. What is a normal day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m Aaron, 43, a lead developer at a tech company that makes software for warehouse scales. I have a master’s degree, and I’m usually the person called when a weight reading and the printed label disagree. I read the device record, trace the code, and speak to the warehouse foreman before we release a patch. I have never used an AI assistant; I want to know which line I can stand behind.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who depends on that work at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My wife, Leena, repairs and alters clothes from a small shop, and our two children are in school. My pay is high and covers most of our mortgage; Leena’s takings change by week. We have eleven months of expenses put aside, and there are plenty of software jobs nearby. I would rather keep a sound job than chase a new tool because everyone else has it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell my team the AI Plateau changes little about checking a scale before it prints a shipping label. A wrong weight can leave a whole truck waiting at the gate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my senior place and our mortgage payment are steady. I have no wish to feed warehouse records into an assistant to save a few minutes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d carry on tracing faults from the device logs and sign each release with the foreman. I’d keep our monthly mortgage payment and put 500 into the reserve while my wage holds. In the first year I’d keep the same two-person check on weight-label changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about my job and the mortgage. A slow week in Leena’s shop is ordinary for us, and eleven months saved covers that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the foreman add to your check?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last month a pallet showed two weights after a cable was replaced. I found a stale reading in the queue, and the foreman checked it on the floor before we cleared the labels.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Leena buy more equipment?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell Leena we can replace the sewing machine when it wears out. I would not buy a new one merely to spend a good quarter of my salary.

say: I expect **AI Plateau** to leave warehouse checks much as they are.
I would keep **foreman checks** before weight-label releases.
think: I expect my **senior wage** to cover our mortgage.
I see no gain from putting **warehouse records** into an assistant.
do: **Trace** scale faults from device logs and sign releases with the foreman.
**Add** 500 monthly to savings while my wage holds.
**Keep** the two-person weight-label check in the first year.
feel: **Calm** about my pay, mortgage and Leena’s variable shop weeks.
S0.quote: A wrong weight can leave a whole truck waiting at the gate.
fieldNote: He trusts **device records** and foremen, not AI tools, and retains a manual release check.
A **high wage** and eleven months saved make ordinary swings in Leena’s shop manageable.

steps.text: Trace warehouse scale faults and keep foreman sign-off on labels
Add 500 monthly to the family reserve while developer pay holds

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say Steady Disruption puts code writing and checking under pressure first, while robots take longer to handle physical scales. I would ask our company to keep a named person responsible for each weight-label release.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think management may stop replacing developers and eventually ask me to oversee more code with fewer people. My pay looks safe this year, but I dislike the smaller path into the trade for younger staff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep the release register and show management three recent faults an automatic code check would have missed. I’d join the local developers’ association if our company stops replacing departing programmers, so we can press for paid apprenticeships. In the first year I’d stay in my lead role while the register still has a human owner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about a trade with no new hands coming through. My own wage is secure for now, but a lead cannot train a junior who was never hired.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a new hire need to see?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would show a new hire how the cable change made an old weight look current. A test can pass while the truck driver is still holding the wrong paper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Leena’s shop alter your plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Leena and I would keep the shop budget separate from my wages. If bookings slow, we would adjust cloth orders before touching the mortgage reserve.

say: I expect **Steady Disruption** to pressure code writing before physical scales.
I would demand **named release responsibility** for each label change.
think: I expect my **lead pay** to hold this year despite fewer hires.
I worry **paid apprenticeships** may disappear with junior vacancies.
do: **Keep** a release register and show management three missed scale faults.
**Join** developers’ association if our company stops replacing programmers.
**Stay** in my lead role while a person owns label releases.
feel: **Uneasy** about junior entry, though my own pay looks safe.
S1.quote: A test can pass while the truck driver is still holding the wrong paper.
fieldNote: His **manual register** is a way to demonstrate accountability for real warehouse errors.
He would join an **association only if** departed developers stop being replaced.

steps.text: Keep warehouse release register and show management three missed scale faults
Join developers association if the company stops replacing departing programmers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell colleagues AGI by 2028 could do our software thinking work by 2028. Robots for handling scales come around 2031, but a later robot does not protect my code salary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I expect our company might remove the whole development team, me included. Eleven months saved buys time, not a promise that another nearby firm will still hire programmers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d cancel the planned kitchen extension and keep its deposit against the mortgage. I’d ask for written redundancy terms and an inventory of which scale jobs remain with people. In the first year after 2028, if dismissed, I’d take a verified paid scale-maintenance opening only if its wage covers the mortgage and school costs; otherwise I’d use savings while seeking eligible income help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed about the loss of my wage, and I would sleep badly until we knew the terms. The extension can wait, but the mortgage cannot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the children about the kitchen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the children the kitchen stays as it is. I would not promise that maintaining scales is safe work until a company offers real hours and pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could Leena’s shop replace your wage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Leena’s alterations income would keep coming if customers still need it, but I would not count it as a replacement for my salary. We would review the bank balance together each month.

say: I expect **2028 thinking AI** to threaten code pay before 2031 robots.
I would say **scale maintenance** needs real paid hours before anyone calls it a fallback.
think: I expect **team-wide cuts** could include me within two years.
Our **eleven-month reserve** cannot guarantee a new programming wage if local firms also cut.
do: **Cancel** the kitchen extension and hold its deposit for mortgage payments.
**Request** written redundancy terms and remaining human-scale duties.
**Apply** to real maintenance openings only if wages cover mortgage and school costs; seek eligible help if dismissed.
feel: **Alarmed** about losing the main wage and the mortgage deadline.
S2.quote: Eleven months saved buys time, not a promise that another nearby firm will still hire programmers.
fieldNote: He expects **2028 AGI** to threaten the whole coding team; robot handling arrives later.
He cancels a **kitchen extension** and requires real hours and adequate wages before changing fields.

steps.text: Cancel kitchen extension and hold deposit for mortgage payments
Apply after 2028 dismissal to verified scale-maintenance openings only if pay covers mortgage and school costs
Seek eligible public income help if dismissed after 2028

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2031 still reaches coding before robots handle scales around 2034. Five years lets us learn the true cost of keeping a warehouse running without a developer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I still expect my code wage could disappear. I would try an apprenticeship in physical instrument calibration, but I know robots may reach that work three years after AGI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the scale service firm we already use whether it will offer a paid calibration apprenticeship with supervised site hours. I’d take it only if the written wage plus Leena’s reliable shop takings cover mortgage, school costs and travel; otherwise I would stay employed and keep the reserve. In the first year after 2031, if my code role ends, I’d apply to real calibration posts only where people are still hired despite the coming 2034 robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about losing a strong wage, even with time to ask around. I could learn to set a scale properly, but I cannot pay a mortgage with an unpaid lesson.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What draws you toward calibration?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The service firm’s senior technician showed me a scale drifting after a cold morning. A meter reading is only useful if someone understands why it changed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you count Leena’s takings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Leena would keep her shop hours, but we would count only her usual paid alterations when we compare apprenticeship wages. A full order book in one holiday week is not a yearly salary.

say: I expect **2031 AGI** to reach coding before 2034 robots handle scales.
I would examine **calibration apprenticeships** with actual supervised site hours.
think: I expect my **code wage** could disappear when full thinking AI arrives.
I know **2034 robots** may erode physical calibration work three years later.
do: **Ask** the service firm for a paid, supervised calibration apprenticeship.
**Accept** only if written wage and reliable shop takings cover mortgage, school costs and travel.
**Apply** after 2031 only to actual calibration posts still hiring people.
feel: **Anxious** about wage loss despite five years to explore.
S3.quote: I cannot pay a mortgage with an unpaid lesson.
fieldNote: He explores **physical calibration** through an existing service firm rather than buying an unknown course.
The **written wage gate** uses only reliable shop takings; robots may affect calibration around 2034.

steps.text: Take a paid supervised calibration apprenticeship only if combined reliable income covers mortgage, school and travel
Apply after 2031 only to real calibration posts still hiring despite approaching robots

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell colleagues AGI by 2036 gives us a decade to document the scale faults our code has hidden from customers. Robots handling scales come around 2039; I would not call the equipment side secure forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I expect my salary to hold for several years, but the company may use AI to cut junior jobs long before 2036. I would rather make our maintenance records useful to the next technician than buy a speculative business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep leading releases and put 500 into savings each month while my pay holds. I’d write a plain repair record for recurring scale faults, with the foreman checking each entry. In the first year after 2036, if my developer post ends, I’d seek an actual paid service role only if its wage covers mortgage and school costs; if no such role exists, I’d use savings while we decide which family costs to change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about what the children will find when they enter work. My own job and the mortgage look safe now, which gives me time to record what people still need to know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the repair notes qualify you for a new job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not pretend my notes are a new trade by themselves. A service firm would have to show a paid vacancy and training before I leave a secure salary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you expand Leena’s shop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell Leena to keep the shop as hers, not turn it into our emergency career plan. We have enough saved to make decisions in order instead of selling her equipment at the first warning.

say: I see **2036 AGI** as time to document faults before code work changes.
I know **2039 robots** could affect equipment work later.
think: I expect my **current wage** to hold for several years.
I worry **junior jobs** may shrink well before 2036.
do: **Keep** leading releases and writing foreman-checked repair records.
**Seek paid service work** after 2036 only for real trained vacancies covering family bills; otherwise use savings and review costs.
feel: **Uneasy** about children’s prospects, with my own pay safe now.
S4.quote: A service firm would have to show a paid vacancy and training before I leave a secure salary.
fieldNote: His **repair records** keep practical fault knowledge visible without changing his job today.
A **service move** depends on an actual vacancy, training and pay that covers family bills.

steps.text: Keep leading warehouse releases and write foreman-checked scale repair records
Save 500 monthly while developer pay holds
Seek trained service vacancy after 2036 with family-covering wage; otherwise use savings and review costs

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most. It could take the team before I can find out whether calibration firms still hire. Clear redundancy terms, a paid opening with enough hours, and time to use our savings would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who signs the label when a warehouse scale and the software disagree. A clean screen does not weigh a truck.

headlineQuote: A clean screen does not weigh a truck.
portrait: Aaron is a **43-year-old lead developer** with a master’s degree, high pay and eleven months saved.
He has **never used AI** and checks warehouse scale software against device records and foremen.
His wife’s **alterations shop** brings variable income, while his wage carries the mortgage and children’s costs.
He explores **paid calibration work** only with supervised training, adequate wages and real posts.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove his entire coding team before he can test another trade.
whatWouldHelp: **Clear redundancy terms**, a paid opening with enough hours and time to use savings would help.
